title: Filtering, projection, ordering, grouping and joins
body: `Where` filters, `Select` projects each element (optionally with its index), and `SelectMany` flattens a sequence of sequences. `OrderBy`/`OrderByDescending` sort by a key, `ThenBy` adds tie-breakers; LINQ sorting is stable. `Order()` and `OrderDescending()` (.NET 7) sort by the elements themselves.

`GroupBy(key)` produces `IGrouping<TKey, TElement>` objects, each with a `Key` and its elements. `ToDictionary` and `ToLookup` build indexes; `ToDictionary` throws on duplicate keys while `ToLookup` allows several values per key.

`Join(inner, outerKey, innerKey, result)` is an inner join that matches elements with equal keys using hashing. `GroupJoin` gives each outer element its group of matches. .NET 10 adds `LeftJoin` and `RightJoin`, so an outer join no longer needs the `GroupJoin` + `SelectMany` + `DefaultIfEmpty` pattern; unmatched elements get `null`/default for the other side.

Query syntax (`from c in customers where c.Active orderby c.Name select c.Name`) compiles to the same method calls. It reads well for joins and `let` clauses; method syntax covers every operator. Mix them freely.
Check sort keys for ties, choose ToLookup when keys repeat, and in outer joins check how the code handles the missing side.

challenge: Using the same customers and orders, list each country with the total order amount of its customers (0 when none), sorted by total descending then country.
question: Which .NET 10 operator keeps outer elements that have no match in the inner sequence?
reasoning: Join is an inner join. LeftJoin passes null/default for the missing inner element, replacing the GroupJoin + DefaultIfEmpty idiom.
